summary: Fontana sprawls across 43 square miles of Inland Empire valley floor at the base of the San Gabriel Mountains, and that footprint matters — it's physically larger than San Francisco, yet at roughly 5,000 people per square mile it has the density of a mid-sized suburb, which means long blocks of residential tracts punctuated by wide commercial arterials rather than any cohesive walkable center. The city is a genuine logistics powerhouse: its position along the I-10 and I-15 corridors, plus proximity to massive distribution hubs, makes warehousing and freight a dominant employer, and the Auto Club Speedway (now closed for redevelopment into a mixed-use project) has been the city's most recognizable landmark for decades. A median home price of $558,500 against a median household income of $98,187 yields a price-to-income ratio around 5.7 — stretched but not impossible compared to coastal Southern California, and monthly rents averaging $1,733 remain accessible to households near that median. The climate is classic inland basin: 9.7 hours of daily sunshine, summer highs that routinely push well past the 76°F annual average into triple digits, and dry winters with cool nights around 54°F — air conditioning isn't optional. The San Gabriel foothills offer trail access to the north, but daily green space within city limits is fragmented, and most errands require a car. Fontana is, at its core, a place where proximity to warehouse-sector employment and relative affordability exist in direct tension with heat, car dependence, and a landscape still catching up to its own rapid growth.
